title: Josh and Chuck's List of Horror Movies that Changed the Genre
summary: Josh and Chuck count down horror movies that changed the genre, based on a Grabster (Gravster-style list cited as Grabster) article plus their own additions. They cover The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari (1920) and German Expressionism, Blood Feast (1963) and gore cinema, Night of the Living Dead (1968) and the modern zombie, The Exorcist (1973) and demonic possession films, Jaws (1975) and the summer blockbuster release, Halloween (1978) and the slasher genre, The Blair Witch Project (1999) and found footage, Scream (1996) and meta horror, and Psycho (1960) and the mid-film twist. The episode closes with a tour announcement, small talk about recent horror films, and a listener mail segment on Gen X nostalgia and Schoolhouse Rock.
topics: movies that changed the horror genre

segments.title: Tour dates and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck announce 2017 tour dates, chat about Malcolm in the Middle and cleaning, and set up the episode title and premise: a Grabster list of horror films that changed the genre, with Josh and Chuck's additions.

segments.title: Horror movie talk and Toby's film The Ghost Story
segments.summary: The hosts plug their friend Toby's producing work on The Ghost Story, released by A24, and discuss recent horror films like The Witch, The Blackcoat's Daughter, It Comes at Night, and Get Out.

segments.title: The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari and German Expressionism
segments.summary: The 1920 German film is called the first horror movie. The hosts discuss its angular, surreal sets and shadows, its link to German Expressionism and World War One, and its influence on later horror.

segments.title: Blood Feast and gore cinema
segments.summary: Blood Feast (1963), directed by Herschel Gordon Lewis and produced by David F. Friedman, is described as a low-budget, poorly made film that showed explicit gore on screen for the first time. The hosts cover its budget, box office, and influence, and mention the Grand Guignol theater in Paris.

segments.title: Break before Night of the Living Dead
segments.summary: A short break in the episode before the discussion of Night of the Living Dead.

segments.title: Night of the Living Dead and the modern zombie
segments.summary: George Romero's 1968 film, shot in black and white in Pittsburgh on a small budget, is credited with establishing the modern flesh-eating zombie. The hosts discuss its Black lead actor cast without making race the story, Roger Ebert's 1969 review of a children's audience reacting, the film's allegorical readings, its sequels, and the killing off of its hero.

segments.title: The Exorcist and demonic horror
segments.summary: The 1973 film based on William Peter Blatty's novel is discussed for its box office and Best Picture nomination, its impact on audiences, religious controversy, possible intergenerational conflict themes, and the pea soup effect. Filming locations such as the Exorcist stairs in Washington, D.C. are mentioned.

segments.title: Jaws and the summer blockbuster
segments.summary: Spielberg's 1975 Jaws is discussed for its troubled shoot, the mechanical shark nicknamed Bruce, its wide release on 435 screens, heavy marketing, and early hit status as a film earning $100 million. The hosts debate whether it is horror or adventure.

segments.title: Halloween and the slasher genre
segments.summary: John Carpenter's 1978 Halloween is credited with establishing the slasher genre through its faceless killer Michael Myers, the Captain Kirk mask, Carpenter's score, and its box office success. Earlier slashers such as Black Christmas and The Town That Dreaded Sundown are mentioned.

segments.title: The Blair Witch Project and found footage
segments.summary: The 1999 film is credited with popularizing found footage through its viral website and the rumor that it was real. The hosts mention earlier found-footage films Mondo Cane and Cannibal Holocaust and the co-directors Eduardo Sanchez and Daniel Myrick.

segments.title: Scream and meta horror
segments.summary: Scream, written by Kevin Williamson, is discussed as a box office hit that started the meta horror subgenre, which is self-referential about horror tropes. Casting trivia (Drew Barrymore, Neve Campbell) and the Weinstein mask are mentioned. Other meta films such as Tucker and Dale vs. Evil, Zombieland, and Cabin in the Woods are noted.

segments.title: Psycho and Ed Gein
segments.summary: Hitchcock's 1960 Psycho is credited with changing horror through the mid-film killing of its lead, Janet Leigh's character, and the reveal of its monster. The hosts discuss its basis in Ed Gein's crimes, the Bates house, and the Hitchcock biopics. Knowl interjects with a note that Anthony Perkins directed The Blackcoat's Daughter and also made The Pretty Little Thing That Lives in the House.

segments.title: Listener mail: Gen X nostalgia theory
segments.summary: Listener Eric proposes that Gen X is nostalgic for pop culture because of heavy children's marketing in the 1970s and 1980s, not because of Schoolhouse Rock as Josh had suggested. The hosts respond and invite more listener theories.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck directs listeners to HowStuffWorks for more topics.
